repo: https://github.com/sharevb/it-tools
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: sharevb/it-tools:2026.7.11
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.small
  flavor_id: "2"
  database: none, and that is deliberate. This app has no server-side store at all; deploy_compose already defaults to database 'compose', which is correct here
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0174
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: it-tools
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ READ THIS FIRST, IT CHANGES WHAT YOU ARE DEPLOYING. IT Tools is a STATIC FRONT END and its image is not a server. The Dockerfile production stage is FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine with the built bundle copied into /usr/share/nginx/html, and nginx.conf contains nothing but a listen directive, two headers, an /assets/ rule and an SPA fallback: no auth_basic, no proxy_pass, no application process. There is no backend, no database, no upload endpoint, no session and NO ACCOUNTS OF ANY KIND. Every tool runs in the visitor's browser and NOTHING IS STORED SERVER-SIDE. That is why this is the cheapest entry in the library: one small VM, no managed database, and nothing on the server that a redeploy or a stranger can destroy."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: NOBODY, EVER. THIS APP HAS NO ACCOUNTS. There is no signup form, no install wizard, no first-user-is-owner rule, no admin panel and no default password, because there is no server-side code to hold a session. So there is no ownership race to lose and no registration setting to close afterwards. WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH IS EVERYTHING: the entire tool set, to anyone who has the URL, and that is the app working as designed rather than a misconfiguration. Nobody can read anybody else's data through it because the server holds none. Say this to the user in plain words before they approve the spend: this deploy puts a public utility on a public hostname. The 8 random characters in the generated hostname are obscurity, not a password."
  - "⛔ IF THE USER NEEDS IT PRIVATE, DECIDE THAT BEFORE DEPLOYING, BECAUSE THE IMAGE CANNOT DO IT. There is no environment variable, no config file and no build flag that adds a login: verified by reading nginx.conf (no auth_basic) and docker-entrypoint.d/, which contains exactly two scripts, one about read-only filesystems and one about IPv6, neither about authentication. Upstream's own README says so in its 'To add authentication' section: put forward-auth on a reverse proxy in front of it. ⚠️ The BASIC_AUTH variable you will see in docker-with-services/docker-compose.yml is consumed by the COMPANION services in that sample, not by the it-tools image, and this recipe does not deploy those. So the honest options are: accept a public utility, or do not deploy it this way."
  - "⛔ DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Upstream's own README, under 'Build requirements', says the build needs around 16 GB of RAM and that below it you get out-of-memory and node allocation failures. Every flavor in this library's normal range would fail. The published image already ran that build for you: pull it, and never pass a build context or a git repo for this entry."
  - "⛔ PIN THE IMAGE, AND NOTE THAT THE IMAGE TAG HAS NO LEADING v WHILE THE GIT TAG DOES. The GitHub release is v2026.7.11 (2026-07-11); the image tag is 2026.7.11 on BOTH registries. Verified on 2026-08-17: sharevb/it-tools has 24 tags on Docker Hub, ghcr.io/sharevb/it-tools has 27, and 2026.7.11 is the newest version tag on each. Typing the v gets you a manifest-unknown error. ⚠️ latest is NOT the release: it is rebuilt on every push to the default branch and was last rebuilt 2026-08-16, a month after 2026.7.11. Upstream's root compose ships the image on the rolling latest tag together with pull_policy: always; DROP BOTH. A rolling tag plus always-pull means the app can change under the user on any restart. There are also latest-en (English only) and *-baseurl-it-tools (built for serving under a /it-tools/ subfolder) tags; neither is what you want here."
  - "⛔ PORT 8080, NOT 80, AND THE README CALLS THIS A BREAKING CHANGE. The base image is nginx-unprivileged, so the container listens on 8080. The Dockerfile sets ENV PORT=8080 and EXPOSE $PORT, and nginx.conf listens on \"${PORT}\", so PORT is a genuine override if you ever need one. Publish 8080 on the VM and pass 8080 to deploy_compose. Any recipe or tutorial that maps 8080:80 is from before that change and produces a container that never answers."
  - "⛔ HTTPS AND TWO HEADERS ARE LOAD-BEARING HERE, SO DO NOT MOUNT YOUR OWN nginx.conf. Several tools use the browser's WebCrypto API (the PGP ones, per the README's own 'HTTPS is recommended' section), which browsers expose only on a secure origin, and the WebAssembly-backed tools need the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy require-corp headers that nginx.conf adds. redu terminates TLS on the *.redu.cloud hostname, so both hold out of the box. The README suggests mounting your own nginx.conf as an IPv6 workaround: DO NOT. You would drop those two headers and the SPA fallback, and the failure mode is an opaque browser error in a handful of tools rather than anything in a log. The IPv6 problem it describes is already solved inside the image by docker-entrypoint.d/25-remove-ipv6-listen-if-unavailable.sh, which removes the IPv6 listen when /proc/net/if_inet6 is absent."
  - "⛔ ANYTHING YOU MOUNT INTO /usr/share/nginx/html IS SERVED TO THE PUBLIC. That directory is the web root, and it is where every one of upstream's optional customisation files goes: tools-filter.json, external-tools.json, home.custom.md and tools-settings.json. So a settings file is a PUBLISHED file. ⚠️ Upstream's own docker-with-services/tools-settings.json contains a literal user:password pair for its companion services, in that exact directory. Mounting a file of that shape onto a public hostname publishes the credential. NEVER put a secret in any file you mount there. tools-filter.json is genuinely useful and safe: it takes includeToolsFilterRegex, excludeToolsFilterRegex, includeCategoryFilterRegex and excludeCategoryFilterRegex, and it is the right way to hide the tools this recipe cannot make work."
  - "⛔ DO NOT DEPLOY docker-with-services/docker-compose.yml. IT PUTS ROOT ON THE VM BEHIND AN HTTP PORT. That sample adds five companion containers, and two of them must never sit on a public hostname: sharevb/docker-image-download-server mounts /var/run/docker.sock, which is root on the VM to anyone who can reach it, and sharevb/cors-anywhere is an open forwarding proxy that would let strangers relay requests through your instance, including into redu's private network. This recipe deploys THE ONE STATIC SERVICE and nothing else. THE CONSEQUENCE, and tell the user rather than letting them find it: the tools that need those services will appear in the UI and will not work. The README names them: HTTPS and DNS tools, Ping, HTML to PDF, Docker Image Download, Multi Links Download, Short URL Expander and the TCP/UDP port tester. Hide them with tools-filter.json, or leave them and explain."
  - "THERE IS NO SECRET TO SET AND NO SILENT SQLITE FALLBACK, WHICH IS UNUSUAL FOR THIS LIBRARY AND IS WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD BECAUSE YOU WILL GO LOOKING. Checked the whole tree: there is no .env, no .env.example, no encryption key, no session secret and no app key anywhere in the repo, because there is no server-side state to protect. Nothing is destroyed by a redeploy, because nothing is kept. Do NOT pass database:'managed'; there is no process in this stack that speaks SQL, and a managed Postgres would be a second VM on the bill that nothing ever connects to. deploy_compose already defaults to database 'compose', which is correct here."
  - "NO VOLUME EITHER, AND THAT IS THE ENTIRE DATA STORY. Nothing needs persisting: the image is read-only content and the container writes nothing you want back. The only durable thing this deployment owns is its hostname. delete_deployment destroys the VM and loses nothing, and there is no delete_database to remember afterwards because there is no database. That is the whole teardown story, and it is worth stating plainly since every other entry in this library has a different one."
  - "THE DEFAULT BRANCH IS chore/all-my-stuffs, NOT main OR master. From the repo metadata, and it is a fork-specific quirk that costs ten minutes. Every raw.githubusercontent.com URL you build against main or master 404s, and so does any documentation link you assemble by hand. Use the branch name or a tag."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO RUNTIME NUMBER. Checked the README, the Dockerfile and all four compose files: the only memory figure anywhere is the 16 GB needed to BUILD, which is irrelevant once you pull. m1.small (1 vCPU / 2 GB, 20 GB disk) is reasoning from 'nginx serving a prebuilt static bundle with no interpreter, no database process and nothing else on the VM', not a measurement. It fits the no-card free trial. Disk never grows, because nothing is written. One detail already handled for you: the Dockerfile sets NGINX_ENTRYPOINT_WORKER_PROCESSES_AUTOTUNE=1 with a comment explaining that nginx's default worker_processes auto counts the HOST's cores and would OOM-kill a small container; do not override it. Measure the real idle figure on your run and write it back."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.017/hr, roughly GBP 13 a month, with no database on the bill because the app has no server-side store; fits the no-card free trial) AND the fact that the URL will be usable by anyone who has it, then WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '2' (m1.small), port 8080, and NO database parameter. plan_deploy wants to upsize a compose stack to m1.large, which is the right default for things that BUILD from source and wrong here, since the image is pulled: passing flavor_id '2' holds m1.small."

GPL-3.0 has NO section 13 network clause, unlike AGPL, so simply hosting an unmodified instance for other people is not distribution and triggers no source-offer obligation. If you MODIFY the app and then distribute your build or your image, you must offer the corresponding source under the GPL. Note also that this is sharevb's fork of CorentinTh/it-tools, which is where its extra tools come from; the fork is what the pinned image is built from."

# Self-host IT Tools on redu

The whole developer-utility belt on your own EU machine and your own domain: JSON and YAML
converters, hash and HMAC, JWT, UUID, regex, cron, colour, encoding, PGP, QR codes and several
hundred more. One small container behind TLS.

About GBP 0.017/hour, roughly GBP 13 a month. There is no managed database on the bill, because
this app has no server-side store to put in one. It is the cheapest entry in this library. Inside
the no-card free trial.

## Read this before you deploy, because it decides whether you want it

IT Tools is a **static front end**. Its image is nginx serving a prebuilt bundle: no backend, no
database, no upload endpoint, no login and no admin account. Every tool computes **in your
browser**, and nothing you paste into it is stored on the server.

Two things follow, and they are the entire trade:

1. **Nothing on the server can leak, because nothing is on the server.** No database to protect,
   no secret to rotate, no account for a stranger to claim, nothing lost in a redeploy.
2. **Anyone with the URL can use it.** There is no way to add a password inside this deploy;
   upstream's answer is to put forward-auth on a reverse proxy in front. The eight random
   characters in the generated hostname are obscurity, not a password.

If that second point is not acceptable, decide it now rather than after the VM exists.

## What this deploys

- **IT Tools** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.small VM. Port 8080 in the container

### Two things to know before you approve

**This deploy puts a public utility on a public hostname.** IT Tools is a static front end — no backend, no accounts, no signup, no admin panel, no default password. There is no environment variable or config file that adds a login; upstream's only answer is forward-auth on a reverse proxy in front of it. **Anyone with the URL gets the entire tool set.** The 8 random characters in the hostname are obscurity, not a password. If it needs to be private, that decision has to happen now rather than after the VM exists.

**Nothing on the server can leak, because nothing is on the server.** Every tool computes in the visitor's browser. No database to protect, no secret to rotate, nothing lost in a redeploy. Teardown is one `delete_deployment` and there's no database left billing behind it.

They can be hidden later with a `tools-filter.json`.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove this IT Tools is serving, with the image's own nginx config rather than a fallback.
#   ./verify-it-tools.sh it-tools-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = good, 1 = broken, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-it-tools.sh <host>}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE. redu's hostname answers 502 from its proxy for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the
#    container starts, and an error page passes every "did it NOT do X" check below by accident.
code=$(curl -sSL -D "$TMP/head" -o "$TMP/index" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/ answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/ answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove IT Tools is what is on this hostname, not something else.
if ! grep -q '<title>IT Tools' "$TMP/index"; then
  inconclusive "/ returned 200 but its HTML is not IT Tools'."
fi
echo "OK: IT Tools is serving."

# 3. THE CROSS-ORIGIN HEADERS. nginx.conf adds both. The base image's stock welcome config does
#    not, so their absence means the image's own config never got rendered and the
#    WebAssembly-backed tools will fail in the browser with an opaque error.
if grep -qi '^cross-origin-embedder-policy: *require-corp' "$TMP/head" \
   && grep -qi '^cross-origin-opener-policy: *same-origin' "$TMP/head"; then
  echo "OK: COOP and COEP are set, so the image's own nginx config is live."
else
  echo "FAIL: the cross-origin headers are missing, so this is not serving with nginx.conf." >&2
  echo "Do not mount your own nginx.conf over the image's; the WASM-backed tools need those two." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. POSITIVE CONTROL FOR THE CHECK BELOW: a REAL hashed asset must be served, or the 404 test
#    that follows proves nothing at all.
asset=$(grep -oE '/assets/[A-Za-z0-9._-]+\.(js|css)' "$TMP/index" | head -1 || true)
if [ -z "$asset" ]; then
  inconclusive "found no hashed /assets/ path in the served HTML, so the next check has no control."
fi
code=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST$asset")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "a real build asset ($asset) answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi
echo "OK: hashed build assets are served."

# 5. THE ASSERTION. A MISSING chunk must 404. Without nginx.conf's try_files rule it falls through
#    to the SPA fallback and is served as index.html with a 200, which the browser rejects with an
#    opaque MIME error instead of a plain, debuggable 404.
code=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/assets/no-such-chunk-here.js")
case "$code" in
  404)
    echo "OK: a missing chunk 404s instead of falling through to index.html."
    exit 0
    ;;
  200)
    echo "FAIL: a nonexistent /assets/ path answered 200, so index.html is being served for it." >&2
    echo "The SPA fallback is swallowing missing chunks. Deep links will break confusingly." >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
  *)
    inconclusive "the missing-chunk probe answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
    ;;
esac

inconclusive() { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. GATE. redu's hostname answers 502 from its proxy for roughly the first 2.5 minutes while the
#    container starts, and an error page passes every "did it NOT do X" check below by accident.
code=$(curl -sSL -D "$TMP/head" -o "$TMP/index" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  inconclusive "/ answered 502. That is redu's proxy while the container starts, NOT a pass. Re-run."
fi
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "/ answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Prove IT Tools is what is on this hostname, not something else.
if ! grep -q '<title>IT Tools' "$TMP/index"; then
  inconclusive "/ returned 200 but its HTML is not IT Tools'."
fi
echo "OK: IT Tools is serving."

# 3. THE ASSERTION: is the IMAGE'S OWN config live, or the base image's stock one? The shipped
#    config is a single `location /` with `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html`, so an unknown deep
#    link must come back 200 AND be the IT Tools shell. nginx-unprivileged's stock config has no
#    try_files, so it would 404 here. This is the discriminator the header check used to be.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/deep" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/no-such-route-$$")
if [ "$code" = "200" ] && grep -q '<title>IT Tools' "$TMP/deep"; then
  echo "OK: the SPA fallback serves unknown routes, so the image's own nginx config is live."
elif [ "$code" = "404" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an unknown route 404d, so the SPA fallback is missing." >&2
  echo "This is the base image's stock config, not IT Tools'. Deep links into the app will break." >&2
  exit 1
else
  inconclusive "an unknown route answered HTTP $code, which this script does not recognise."
fi

# 4. A REAL hashed asset must be served.
asset=$(grep -oE '/assets/[A-Za-z0-9._-]+\.(js|css)' "$TMP/index" | head -1 || true)
if [ -z "$asset" ]; then
  inconclusive "found no hashed /assets/ path in the served HTML."
fi
code=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST$asset")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  inconclusive "a real build asset ($asset) answered HTTP $code, not 200."
fi
echo "OK: hashed build assets are served."

# 5. REPORTED, NOT ASSERTED. Tag 2026.7.11 ships all eight add_header lines COMMENTED OUT, so the
#    absence of COOP/COEP is the image working as built - not a misconfiguration and not something
#    a redeploy fixes. It does mean cross-origin isolation is off and SharedArrayBuffer is
#    unavailable, so threaded-WASM tools degrade in the browser with no server-side trace.
if grep -qi '^cross-origin-embedder-policy: *require-corp' "$TMP/head" \
   && grep -qi '^cross-origin-opener-policy: *same-origin' "$TMP/head"; then
  echo "NOTE: COOP and COEP ARE set - this instance is cross-origin isolated."
  echo "      That is NOT stock for 2026.7.11; something is adding them. Check what."
else
  echo "NOTE: COOP/COEP absent, which is EXPECTED on 2026.7.11 (upstream ships them commented out)."
  echo "      crossOriginIsolated is false and SharedArrayBuffer is unavailable, so threaded-WASM"
  echo "      tools may degrade. Everything else, including the WebCrypto/PGP tools, is unaffected."
fi

# 6. REPORTED, NOT ASSERTED. There is no `location /assets/` block in the shipped config, so a
#    missing chunk falls through to index.html with a 200. Only worth knowing about because the
#    browser-side symptom (an opaque MIME error on a stale tab) looks nothing like the cause.
code=$(curl -sSL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/assets/no-such-chunk-here.js")
if [ "$code" = "404" ]; then
  echo "NOTE: a missing chunk 404s. Cleaner than stock 2026.7.11, which has no /assets/ rule."
else
  echo "NOTE: a missing chunk answered $code (index.html via the SPA fallback), which is stock for"
  echo "      this tag. A stale tab requesting an old chunk sees an opaque MIME error; a hard"
  echo "      reload fixes it. Not a broken deploy."
fi
echo "PASS: [REDACTED:value] Tools is up and serving with its own config."
exit 0
